slides.title: Endpoint Threat Auditing: After Prevention Fails
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-53 control family AU (Audit and Accountability) governs this domain, most notably AU-2 (Event Logging) and AU-9 (Protection of Audit Information).

Exam tip: Frame auditing explicitly as the detective-control complement to Topics 4.1-4.3's preventive controls.
content_blocks: Topics 4.1–4.3 examined how endpoints are attacked, authenticated, and hardened. This final chapter of Unit 4 addresses what happens after every prior control has already failed and an attacker has gained a foothold: endpoint threat auditing, the practice of systematically recording, protecting, and analyzing security-relevant events generated by an endpoint's OS, applications, and security tooling.

This is the device-level equivalent of the physical intrusion detection concepts from Topic 2.4, assuming prevention will eventually fail and asking how quickly and completely the failure can be reconstructed.

slides.title: Why Logs Exist: The Endpoint's Memory of Itself
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Windows records these events in the Security event log; Linux typically uses auditd alongside syslog.

Misconception: Students often think RAM/process inspection is the primary post-incident evidence source, but by the time an incident is discovered, that's usually gone. The log is what survives.
bullets: Audit log: structured, chronological record of security-relevant events
Logons, privilege escalations, file access, process creation, config changes
Windows: Security event log (Event Viewer); Linux: auditd + syslog
Often the ONLY surviving evidence once the attacker's live session has ended

slides.title: Why Logs Exist: The Endpoint's Memory of Itself
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Windows records these events in the Security event log; Linux typically uses auditd alongside syslog.

Misconception: Students often think RAM/process inspection is the primary post-incident evidence source, but by the time an incident is discovered, that's usually gone. The log is what survives.
content_blocks: Every modern OS maintains an internal audit log of security-relevant activity. This log is the endpoint's own memory of what has happened to it, and for an investigator arriving after an attack has concluded, it is frequently the only surviving evidence of what the attacker actually did, since the live session, network connection, and in-memory artifacts are typically gone by the time an incident is discovered.

choices: Privilege Escalation
Indicator Removal (T1070)

quiz.explanation: Clearing or tampering with logs to erase evidence is classified under T1070, Indicator Removal, with sub-techniques for Windows and Linux/Mac log clearing.

Context: MITRE ATT&CK T1070 (Indicator Removal), sub-techniques T1070.001 and T1070.002.

Exam tip: Name the specific ATT&CK technique ID when discussing log tampering on an FRQ.
content_blocks: Because logs are often the only durable evidence of an intrusion, a rational attacker has a strong incentive to tamper with or delete them as one of the final steps of an attack, classified under MITRE ATT&CK technique category Indicator Removal (T1070), with sub-techniques T1070.001 (Clear Windows Event Logs) and T1070.002 (Clear Linux or Mac System Logs).

An attacker with local administrative privileges on Windows can clear the Security event log entirely using built-in tools; an attacker with root on Linux can truncate or delete local syslog files, in both cases erasing the evidence of how they got in, what they did, and where they went next.

slides.title: Log Tampering Is Itself a Detectable Event
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Like a burglar who wipes fingerprints off a doorknob, the act of wiping is itself evidence someone was there who didn't want to be seen.

Exam tip: This professor's-note insight directly explains why Event ID 1102 exists and why it's high-severity.
bullets: Clearing a security log is itself a loggable, highly suspicious event
Legitimate admins essentially never have routine business reason to clear the whole log
A 'log cleared' event should be treated as near-certain indicator of compromise
This insight underlies Windows Event ID 1102 (covered in Section II)

slides.title: Log Tampering Is Itself a Detectable Event
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Like a burglar who wipes fingerprints off a doorknob, the act of wiping is itself evidence someone was there who didn't want to be seen.

Exam tip: This professor's-note insight directly explains why Event ID 1102 exists and why it's high-severity.
content_blocks: A crucial insight this chapter builds toward: the act of clearing or deleting a security log is, itself, a loggable and highly suspicious security event. A legitimate administrator essentially never has a routine business reason to clear the entire Security event log on a production endpoint. When a SOC sees an event indicating the log was cleared, that event itself should be treated as a near-certain indicator of compromise, not dismissed as routine maintenance.

slides.title: The Core Defense: Get the Logs Off the Endpoint
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This 'forward first, delete second' race is why security architects treat log-forwarding latency as a meaningful security metric.

Exam tip: This is the single most important architectural principle in this chapter, center any FRQ answer about endpoint audit defense on it.
bullets: Foundational principle: forward every log event, in near-real-time, to a centralized log server
Centralized, secure log server: Syslog collector or full SIEM, physically/logically separate
If log already left the endpoint, deleting the local copy accomplishes nothing
'Forward first, delete second' race -- forwarding latency is a security metric

slides.title: The Core Defense: Get the Logs Off the Endpoint
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This 'forward first, delete second' race is why security architects treat log-forwarding latency as a meaningful security metric.

Exam tip: This is the single most important architectural principle in this chapter, center any FRQ answer about endpoint audit defense on it.
content_blocks: The foundational architectural principle of endpoint threat auditing follows directly from the attacker's incentive: if logs are only ever stored locally, an attacker who compromises the endpoint can simply delete the evidence. The defense is to continuously forward every log event, in as close to real time as possible, to a centralized, secure log server, a Syslog collector or full SIEM platform, physically and logically separated from any single endpoint an attacker might compromise.

If the log has already left the endpoint by the time an attacker attempts to clear it, deleting the local copy accomplishes nothing; the centrally forwarded copy is untouched. This is the single most important architectural decision in endpoint threat auditing, and the device-level parallel to the 'assume prevention will eventually fail' philosophy from Topic 2.4.

slides.title: Key Windows Security Event IDs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Event IDs are stable across Windows versions for the same event category, making them a reliable basis for detection rules shared across a heterogeneous fleet.

Exam tip: Memorize 4625 = failed logon, 4624 = successful logon, 1102 = audit log cleared. These three are the highest-yield facts in this chapter.
bullets: Event ID 4625: failed logon attempt
Event ID 4624: successful logon
Event ID 1102: the Security event log itself was cleared
Event IDs are stable across Windows versions -- reliable basis for detection rules

slides.title: Key Windows Security Event IDs
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Event IDs are stable across Windows versions for the same event category, making them a reliable basis for detection rules shared across a heterogeneous fleet.

Exam tip: Memorize 4625 = failed logon, 4624 = successful logon, 1102 = audit log cleared. These three are the highest-yield facts in this chapter.
content_blocks: Windows records security events using numeric Event IDs that allow analysts and tooling to filter and correlate on precise event categories. Event ID 4625 ('An account failed to log on') records every failed authentication attempt, a burst against a single account in a short window is a classic brute-force indicator. Event ID 4624 records a successful logon and, correlated against a preceding burst of 4625 failures, can indicate a successful brute-force compromise. Event ID 1102 specifically records that the Security event log itself was cleared, directly implementing the detection principle from Section 1, since this event is generated by the very act of an attacker attempting to erase their tracks.

slides.title: Correlated Brute-Force Detection: SIEM Rule Logic
slides.speaker_notes:
Misconception: Alerting on 4625 alone floods the SOC with false positives from ordinary user typos. The value is in the CORRELATION between failure burst and subsequent success.

Exam tip: A strong FRQ answer names both event IDs AND explains why correlating them beats single-event alerting.
bullets: Single-event alerting on 4625 alone generates excessive false positives
Correlation: 10+ 4625 failures within 5 min, SAME account/source IP
Followed by a 4624 success within 2 min AFTER the failure burst
High-confidence indicator of successful brute-force / credential-stuffing

slides.title: Correlated Brute-Force Detection: SIEM Rule Logic
slides.speaker_notes:
Misconception: Alerting on 4625 alone floods the SOC with false positives from ordinary user typos. The value is in the CORRELATION between failure burst and subsequent success.

Exam tip: A strong FRQ answer names both event IDs AND explains why correlating them beats single-event alerting.
content_blocks: A correlated detection rule flags any account accumulating a high volume of Event ID 4625 failures in a short window, followed by an eventual Event ID 4624 success for that same account, as a high-confidence indicator of a successful brute-force compromise rather than routine mistyped-password activity.

slides.title: Correlated Brute-Force Detection: SIEM Rule Logic
slides.speaker_notes:
Misconception: Alerting on 4625 alone floods the SOC with false positives from ordinary user typos. The value is in the CORRELATION between failure burst and subsequent success.

Exam tip: A strong FRQ answer names both event IDs AND explains why correlating them beats single-event alerting.

code_block.content:
# SIEM correlation rule -- detect brute-force followed by success
[detection_rule]
name            = "Brute-force-then-success"
condition_1     = EventID=4625 COUNT>=10 WITHIN 5m SAME account,source_ip
condition_2     = EventID=4624 WITHIN 2m AFTER condition_1 SAME account
severity        = HIGH
action          = ALERT-SOC + AUTO-DISABLE-ACCOUNT-PENDING-REVIEW

# Rationale: 10+ failed logons in 5 minutes followed by a success for
# the same account is a strong indicator that a brute-force or
# credential-stuffing attempt eventually guessed correctly, rather
# than a legitimate user simply mistyping their password repeatedly.

slides.title: Linux Auditing: auditd and Syslog
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Common Criteria and many U.S. federal compliance frameworks (FIPS 140, DISA STIG hardening) mandate specific auditd rule sets as a baseline. Syslog carries standardized severity levels (0-7) and facility codes.

Analogy: auditd is to Linux what the Security event log is to Windows; syslog is the transport that gets it off-host.
bullets: auditd: kernel-level auditing subsystem, granular, rule-based
syslog (RFC 5424): standardized protocol for local + remote log forwarding
Root attacker can disable auditd, delete /var/log/auth.log, clear journal
Production fleets forward syslog output to a remote server continuously

slides.title: Linux Auditing: auditd and Syslog
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Common Criteria and many U.S. federal compliance frameworks (FIPS 140, DISA STIG hardening) mandate specific auditd rule sets as a baseline. Syslog carries standardized severity levels (0-7) and facility codes.

Analogy: auditd is to Linux what the Security event log is to Windows; syslog is the transport that gets it off-host.
content_blocks: Linux systems achieve equivalent auditing through two complementary subsystems: auditd, which provides granular kernel-level event auditing, and syslog, the standardized protocol (RFC 5424) used to forward events to a remote collector. A local attacker with root privileges can disable auditd, delete /var/log/auth.log, or clear the systemd journal, the same local file log deletion threat vector this chapter centers on, which is exactly why production Linux fleets forward syslog output to a remote server continuously rather than relying on local retention alone.

slides.title: Tamper-Evident Logging: WORM Storage
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Many regulatory and forensic chain-of-custody frameworks explicitly require WORM-compliant storage for audit logs subject to legal or compliance retention requirements.

Exam tip: WORM addresses a SECOND-ORDER risk beyond simple centralization, don't conflate the two.
bullets: Centralizing logs defends against local endpoint compromise only
A privileged attacker who compromises the central log server can still tamper
Write-Once, Read-Many (WORM) storage: data can be written once, never modified/deleted
Enforced at hardware/filesystem level, even against a full admin account

slides.title: Tamper-Evident Logging: WORM Storage
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Many regulatory and forensic chain-of-custody frameworks explicitly require WORM-compliant storage for audit logs subject to legal or compliance retention requirements.

Exam tip: WORM addresses a SECOND-ORDER risk beyond simple centralization, don't conflate the two.
content_blocks: Centralizing logs off-host defends against local deletion, but a sufficiently privileged attacker who also compromises the central log server itself could still tamper with historical records. Advanced log architectures defend against this second-order risk using write-once storage (WORM), a storage medium that permits data to be written once but never subsequently modified or deleted, even by an administrator with otherwise full privileges over the storage system.

slides.title: Tamper-Evident Logging: Cryptographic Chaining
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Conceptually identical to the block-linking mechanism used in blockchain technology, applied here purely for tamper-evidence rather than for distributed consensus.

Exam tip: Pair this with WORM storage as the two techniques closing the 'privileged attacker on the log server' gap.
bullets: Cryptographic log chaining: each entry includes hash of the previous entry
Conceptually identical to blockchain block-linking, applied for tamper-evidence not consensus
Altering any historical entry breaks the hash chain for every subsequent entry
Tampering becomes mathematically detectable during an integrity verification pass

slides.title: Tamper-Evident Logging: Cryptographic Chaining
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Conceptually identical to the block-linking mechanism used in blockchain technology, applied here purely for tamper-evidence rather than for distributed consensus.

Exam tip: Pair this with WORM storage as the two techniques closing the 'privileged attacker on the log server' gap.
content_blocks: Cryptographic log chaining is a tamper-evidence technique in which each new log entry incorporates a cryptographic hash of the prior entry, meaning any retroactive alteration of a historical record breaks the hash chain for every subsequent entry and becomes immediately, mathematically detectable during an integrity verification pass.

slides.title: Tamper-Evident Logging: Cryptographic Chaining
slides.speaker_notes:
Analogy: Conceptually identical to the block-linking mechanism used in blockchain technology, applied here purely for tamper-evidence rather than for distributed consensus.

Exam tip: Pair this with WORM storage as the two techniques closing the 'privileged attacker on the log server' gap.

slides.title: Centralization Alone Is Not Sufficient

quiz.question: An organization forwards all logs to a central Syslog server, but any administrator can freely edit historical files there. What risk remains, and what best addresses it?
choices: No risk remains; centralization alone is sufficient
The risk of local endpoint deletion is unaddressed; fix by adding more endpoint agents
A privileged attacker on the log server could still tamper with records; address with WORM storage and/or cryptographic hash chaining
The risk is network latency; address by using UDP instead of TCP for syslog
quiz.explanation: Centralization defeats single-endpoint compromise, but a privileged attacker on the log server itself can still tamper with records unless tamper-evident storage (WORM) or cryptographic chaining is added.

slides.speaker_notes:
Misconception: Students frequently stop at 'centralize the logs' and miss the second-order risk of a compromised log server. Full credit requires both layers.

Exam tip: This is the single most commonly missed point on FRQs about this topic, always mention the log-server-compromise scenario.
bullets: Forwarding logs off-host defeats an attacker who compromises only a single endpoint
It does NOT by itself defeat an attacker who also gains admin access to the log server
Tamper-evident techniques (WORM, hash chaining) close this second-order gap
A complete answer must mention both layers, not just 'send logs to a central server'

Tamper-evident techniques (WORM storage, hash chaining) exist specifically to close this second-order gap, and a complete answer describing endpoint audit defense should mention both layers rather than treating 'we send logs to a central server' as a complete solution.

slides.speaker_notes:

content_blocks: Publicly documented incident-response case studies across numerous ransomware and targeted-intrusion investigations consistently report the same late-stage attacker behavior: after achieving their primary objective, attackers frequently attempt to clear Windows Security event logs, delete PowerShell command history, and remove or truncate relevant syslog files, precisely the T1070 'Indicator Removal' technique. Responders investigating these cases repeatedly found that organizations with centralized log forwarding in place BEFORE the intrusion could fully reconstruct the attacker's timeline from the forwarded copies despite local log deletion, while organizations relying solely on local retention lost significant forensic visibility.

slides.title: Pillar 1: Comprehensive, Baseline-Aligned Event Logging
slides.speaker_notes: Misconception: 'We have logging enabled' is not the same as 'we log the right things at the right verbosity.' Default OS logging settings are frequently insufficient.
content_blocks: Endpoints should be configured to log the full baseline of security-relevant events recommended by a recognized hardening standard (such as a DISA STIG or CIS Benchmark audit policy configuration) rather than relying on default, often minimal, out-of-the-box logging settings, directly closing detection gaps that would otherwise exist simply because a relevant event type was never being recorded in the first place.

slides.title: Pillar 2: Immediate Centralized Forwarding
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: A gap in the forwarded log stream is itself a detection signal, it may mean an attacker disabled forwarding before attempting local cleanup.
bullets: Every monitored endpoint forwards its security event stream continuously
Minimal latency directly implements 'forward first, delete second'
Forwarding latency itself should be monitored as a security metric
A sudden gap in received events from an endpoint is itself suspicious

slides.title: Pillar 2: Immediate Centralized Forwarding
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: A gap in the forwarded log stream is itself a detection signal, it may mean an attacker disabled forwarding before attempting local cleanup.
content_blocks: Every monitored endpoint should forward its security event stream continuously to a centralized log server or SIEM with minimal latency, directly implementing the 'forward first, delete second' defense against local log tampering. Forwarding latency should itself be monitored as a security metric, a sudden gap in received events from a given endpoint is itself a suspicious indicator worth investigating.

slides.title: Pillar 3: Tamper-Evident Storage at the Collector
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This pillar directly operationalizes the Section 2 tamper-evidence techniques (WORM, hash chaining) as a hardening requirement, not just a theoretical option.
bullets: The central log server should itself be hardened
Write-once storage configurations and/or cryptographic log chaining
Closes the second-order risk of a privileged attacker reaching the collector
Prevents retroactive alteration of historical records without detection

content_blocks: The central log server should itself be hardened using write-once storage configurations and/or cryptographic log chaining, closing the second-order risk that a sufficiently privileged attacker who reaches the central collector could retroactively alter historical records without detection.

Multiple related signals within a defined time window

slides.title: Pillar 4: Correlated Detection Over Single-Event Alerting
slides.speaker_notes: Context: Alert fatigue was introduced for physical sensors in Topic 2.4 and applies identically here to SIEM analysts.
content_blocks: SOC detection logic should prioritize correlation rules, multiple related signals within a defined time window, over alerting on any single log line in isolation, directly reducing both false-negative risk (a single suspicious-but-ambiguous event being dismissed) and alert fatigue (the same phenomenon documented for physical sensors in Topic 2.4) from high-volume, low-fidelity individual events.

slides.title: Exam Focus: Auditing Completes Unit 4's Defense-in-Depth Model
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This four-topic sequence is likely the single highest-value memorized structure for a Unit 4 synthesis FRQ.
bullets: Harden the endpoint against vulnerabilities in Topic 4.1
Authenticate users strongly per Topic 4.2
Apply the hardening controls of Topic 4.3
Ensure centralized, tamper-evident auditing preserves evidence if all three fail (this chapter)

slides.title: Exam Focus: Auditing Completes Unit 4's Defense-in-Depth Model
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This four-topic sequence is likely the single highest-value memorized structure for a Unit 4 synthesis FRQ.
content_blocks: When asked to design a complete endpoint security scheme spanning this entire unit, a strong answer sequences all four topics: harden the endpoint against the vulnerabilities in Topic 4.1, authenticate users strongly per Topic 4.2, apply the hardening controls of Topic 4.3, and finally ensure that if all three still fail, centralized, tamper-evident auditing (this chapter) preserves the evidence needed to detect the compromise and reconstruct what happened.

slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: These four pillars map one-to-one onto a strong FRQ rubric for 'design an endpoint audit program.'
bullets: Baseline-aligned logging, full event coverage per DISA STIG / CIS Benchmark
Forwarding latency, a monitored security metric, not just an operational one
Hardened collector, WORM + hash chaining applied to the central log server
Correlated detection, the SOC-side application of layered sensing (Topic 2.4)

slides.title: Practice: Interpreting a 4625/4624 Log Excerpt

quiz.question: A SIEM shows 15 Event ID 4625 records for one account within 5 minutes, followed by one Event ID 4624 two minutes later for the same account. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: A user who forgot their password and eventually remembered it
A successful brute-force or credential-stuffing compromise of that account
A misconfigured logging agent double-counting events
Normal single sign-on token refresh behavior
quiz.explanation: A large failure burst immediately followed by a success for the same account is the textbook correlated brute-force detection pattern described in Section 2.

slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: Walk through the two-condition rule explicitly: (1) failure burst count/window/account match, (2) success event within the follow-on window for the same account.
bullets: Given a log excerpt, identify which events indicate a brute-force attempt
Count 4625 events per account within a time window
Check for a following 4624 for the same account
Determine whether this meets the correlation rule threshold

slides.title: Practice: Writing an auditd Rule Concept
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: You are not expected to write exact auditctl syntax on the AP exam, but you should be able to describe WHAT kind of event a baseline auditd rule set should capture and WHY.
bullets: auditd rules target specific kernel-level events (file access, syscalls, privilege changes)
A rule to watch for modification of /etc/passwd is a classic baseline example
Compare to Windows: equivalent to watching a specific registry key or file ACL change
Rule verbosity vs. log volume is a real operational tradeoff

slides.title: Practice: Writing an auditd Rule Concept
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: You are not expected to write exact auditctl syntax on the AP exam, but you should be able to describe WHAT kind of event a baseline auditd rule set should capture and WHY.
content_blocks: A representative auditd rule concept: watch for any write access to /etc/passwd, since unauthorized modification of this file is a strong indicator of local privilege escalation or persistence-establishment activity by an attacker who has gained root or sudo access.

slides.title: Practice: Writing an auditd Rule Concept
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: You are not expected to write exact auditctl syntax on the AP exam, but you should be able to describe WHAT kind of event a baseline auditd rule set should capture and WHY.

code_block.content:
# Example auditd rule (conceptual): watch for writes to /etc/passwd
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k passwd_changes

# -w  : watch this file
# -p wa : trigger on Write and Attribute-change access
# -k  : tag matching events with a searchable key for SIEM correlation

slides.title: Synthesis: The Endpoint Audit Kill Chain View
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This end-to-end kill-chain narrative is the strongest possible structure for a synthesis FRQ asking you to 'trace how an intrusion is detected and preserved as evidence.'
bullets: 1. Attacker compromises endpoint (Topics 4.1-4.3 controls have failed)
2. Attacker acts -- privilege escalation, lateral movement, data access
3. Local + forwarded logs capture each step (Section 2 event IDs)
4. Attacker attempts Indicator Removal (T1070) -- clears local logs (generates 1102)
5. Forwarded copies survive; correlation rules flag both the attack AND the cleanup attempt
6. Tamper-evident storage (WORM/hash chain) ensures the forwarded copies can't be altered either

slides.title: Synthesis: The Endpoint Audit Kill Chain View
slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: This end-to-end kill-chain narrative is the strongest possible structure for a synthesis FRQ asking you to 'trace how an intrusion is detected and preserved as evidence.'
content_blocks: Synthesizing the full chapter into a single narrative: an attacker compromises an endpoint after defeating the controls of Topics 4.1–4.3. As they act, escalating privileges, moving laterally, accessing data, each step generates log events (Section 2's Event IDs, auditd records) that are immediately forwarded to a centralized SIEM. Near the end of the intrusion, the attacker attempts Indicator Removal (T1070), clearing local logs, itself generating a detectable event (1102). Because the logs were already forwarded, the local deletion doesn't erase the evidence; correlation rules flag both the original compromise AND the cleanup attempt. Tamper-evident storage at the collector ensures that even a privileged attacker reaching the log server can't retroactively alter the record.

cover.summary: What a device records about itself, why that record has to leave the machine before an attacker can reach it, how to choose detective controls that match the attack rather than the convenient event, how to judge a detection method by what analysts can actually act on, and how to read a credential attack out of real authentication logs.

cover.notes: Cover slide for Topic 4.4: Detecting Attacks on Devices. What a device records about itself, why that record has to leave the machine before an attacker can reach it, how to choose detective controls that match the attack rather than the convenient event, how to judge a detection method by what analysts can actually act on, and how to read a credential attack out of real authentication logs.

items.text: Explain how attacks against devices are detected: what the operating system and its security tooling record, why that record must be forwarded off the host, and what makes a sequence of events evidence when no single event is.

Determine which controls will detect a given attack against a device — audit policy and the events it enables, off-host forwarding, correlation logic, tamper-evident retention — and state which attacks each would and would not catch.

Evaluate the impact of a detection method: the coverage it gives, the alert volume it creates, whether the people receiving its output can act on it, and what it will still miss — recognising that an untriageable rule lowers detection capability.

Apply detection techniques to authentication log files to identify indicators of password attacks, separating exhaustive guessing against one account from low-and-slow guessing across many, and stating which distinctions the log can and cannot support.

big_idea.text: Endpoint monitoring is a doctor tracking vital signs over time. Any single reading might look normal on its own, but watched together, the pattern reveals an infection before the patient ever notices a symptom.
big_idea.closing: Hold onto this picture — we'll come back to it as the mechanics get more technical.
